one_liner: Research in-memory key-value cache/store over DPDK UDP; 65-77 Mops on tiny items per 16-core server, far above Memcached.
what_it_does: MICA (NSDI'14) is a single-node, partitioned in-memory key-value server. It has a cache mode (circular log, silent eviction) and a store mode (segregated-fit allocator, lossless index), and each mode is built as its own binary. It does not speak the memcached protocol: clients send a custom UDP datagram format, compute the 64-bit keyhash themselves, and choose the target partition by encoding it in the UDP destination port. The repo ships benchmark programs (netbench_server/client, microbench) driven by generated config files, plus an embeddable C table API (mehcached_get/set/delete/increment/test, each taking a caller-supplied keyhash). Keys are capped at 255 bytes, and items that span more than one packet are an explicit non-goal.
how_it_is_fast: It partitions data by keyhash in EREW mode, so each core owns its partitions outright with no locks or cache-line sharing. Clients help the NIC route requests: the Intel Flow Director perfect-match filter sends each packet to the owning core's RX queue based on its UDP port, over DPDK with burst I/O (up to 32 packets) and zero-copy replies built inside the request buffer. In cache mode, items live in a per-partition circular log on hugepages (FIFO, or approximate LRU by re-appending, with no garbage collection). That log is indexed by a lossy set-associative hash index: 15 tag+offset slots per 128-byte bucket, where a collision evicts the oldest entry instead of being resolved, and 48-bit offsets let dangling pointers be detected cheaply. Multi-stage software prefetching overlaps the packet, bucket and log-entry cache misses across a burst, and store mode swaps in segregated fits plus bulk chaining (spare buckets sized at 10% of the main buckets).
when_to_use: You control both clients and servers and can give a cache tier dedicated Intel 10GbE (ixgbe, Flow Director) NICs and hugepages for kernel bypass.

Many tiny or small items (8-64 B values, keys of 255 B or less) under write-heavy or Zipf-skewed traffic where lock-based stores stop scaling. The paper shows MICA holding 65.6-76.9 Mops, losing at most 14% to skew.
Cache semantics are acceptable: silent eviction on a full hash bucket or on log wrap-around is fine for your data.
You need high throughput with a single round trip per request: the paper measured 24-52 us average end-to-end latency while serving tens of Mops.
You want a compact reference implementation (about 12K lines of C) of EREW partitioning, client-steered NIC request direction, and a circular log with a lossy set-associative index.
when_not_to_use: You need a memcached drop-in. It has no memcached text or binary protocol, no TCP, and no client library beyond the benchmark clients, so applications must adopt its UDP format and handle loss and retries themselves.
You need values larger than one packet, multi-get, CAS, range queries, persistence or replication. The paper lists durability and multi-packet items as non-goals.

Cloud VMs, non-Intel NICs or current DPDK. The build links only DPDK's ixgbe PMD and relies on Flow Director and a 2014-era DPDK make-based setup (>= 1.5.0). gen_confs.py hard-codes the paper's testbed (8 server ports, a 16-core server, 12-core clients, 10.0.0.x addresses).

Anything that needs upstream support. master was frozen on 2014-03-03, the isca2015 branch on 2016-01-18, no issue or PR has ever been filed, and Apache-2.0 appears only as README text with no LICENSE file.
Store mode where writes must never fail for lack of space. Spare buckets are fixed at 10% of the main buckets, and once they run out a SET is rejected with an out-of-space error.

integration.dependencies: Intel DPDK >= 1.5.0 (paper used 1.4.1; rte_eal, rte_mempool, rte_ring, rte_mbuf, ethdev, ixgbe PMD), libcrypto, librt, libm, pthread, hugetlbfs mounted at /mnt/huge, cmake >= 2.6, Python 2.7 and bash 4 for config generation
integration.min_toolchain: GNU C with gcc >= 4.6.0 and cmake >= 2.6; repo builds with -O9 -msse4.2 -march=corei7
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux >= 3.2 only (SSE4.2, Nehalem or newer); peak results need a dual-socket NUMA server with Intel 10GbE ixgbe NICs that support Flow Director, plus 2 MiB hugepages
integration.thread_safety: The access mode is set per table at init. EREW gives one core per partition with no synchronization. CREW allows a single writer, with optimistic lock-free readers checking per-bucket 32-bit version counters. CRCW makes writers take per-bucket CAS spinlocks. The server hard-codes these optimizations and cannot switch modes at runtime, and the paper advises avoiding CRCW.

gotchas: Build mode matters. configure_all.sh sets NDEBUG=yes, but a plain `cmake ..` leaves asserts on, and the debug path in mehcached_get deliberately asserts on any value longer than 1500 bytes. With NDEBUG=yes, error paths written as `assert(false)` (such as hugepage allocation failure during table or pool init) print a message and keep going instead of aborting.

Cache mode is lossy by design. A SET into a full 15-slot bucket evicts that bucket's oldest entry even when the log has free space. A GET with a too-small output buffer returns success with a silently truncated value (partial-value handling is marked TODO).
expire_time is stored and echoed back to clients but never enforced by the server (netbench_server.c: 'TODO: use expire_time'), so clients must check staleness themselves.

Log pool sizes are rounded up to the next power of two (and a 2 MiB multiple), so memory use can nearly double. Init also shells out to `rm /mnt/huge/mehcached_shm_*`. basic_types.h does `typedef int bool`, which breaks when included from C++ or alongside stdbool.h.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose MICA over MemC3 (same CMU group, memcached-compatible) or Pelikan/Segcache (a production memcached replacement) only when you own the NIC, the client library and the hardware, and peak tiny-item ops per server is the goal. For anything that has to work with standard clients or on commodity cloud hosts, Pelikan, Dragonfly or Pogocache are the practical choices.
verified_claims_summary: NSDI'14 Fig. 10 tested a dual 8-core Xeon E5-2680 server with eight 10GbE ports, running DPDK 1.4.1 with 16 EREW partitions, 8B/8B items and no client batching. MICA's cache mode served 75.5-76.9 Mops on uniform keys and 65.6-70.5 Mops on Zipf-0.99. Memcached rev 87e2f36, ported to MICA's DPDK stack and at its best with 2 cores, reached 0.7-1.3 Mops, and the next-best system, Masstree, reached 16.5 Mops. The paper does not give the compiler version; the repo's flags are -O9 -msse4.2 -march=corei7. MICA was network-bound (54.9-66.4 Gbps used), so the gap narrows for 16B/64B and 128B/1024B items (8.6-14.6 Mops on the large set). The latency comparison (MICA at 24-52 us) was against stock Memcached on the kernel network stack.
status_note: Abandoned: master was last committed 2014-03-03 and the isca2015 branch 2016-01-18, no issues or PRs have ever been filed, and Apache-2.0 is stated only in the README. It is a copyable C reference to learn from rather than a deployable service, and its C++ successor efficient/mica2 (DPDK 16.11, g++ >= 5.3) has also been idle since 2017.
